payload.rationale: Without recent inflation data for late 2026, the estimate relies on historical base rates for monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) changes in a normalized economic environment. The Federal Reserve targets a 2% annual inflation rate, which corresponds to an average monthly increase of slightly under 0.2%. However, monthly readings are volatile. An increase of strictly more than 0.2% (meaning 0.3% or higher on a single-decimal basis) occurs roughly 40-50% of the time when annual inflation is between 2% and 3%. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is if the economy is experiencing a deflationary trend or a recession in late 2026, pushing monthly CPI changes consistently to 0.2% or lower. The strongest reason this estimate could be too low is if inflation has re-accelerated due to supply shocks, expansionary fiscal policy, or resilient consumer demand, making 0.3% or higher readings the norm.
limitations: No current macroeconomic data or inflation trends for 2026 are available.
Uncertainty regarding whether the Federal Reserve has achieved or maintained its 2% inflation target by late 2026.
